title: Division of labor
objective: Describe the rough functional split between vagal and spinal visceral afferents.

steps.title: Different jobs, roughly
steps.body: As a first approximation: **vagal** afferents carry physiological 'housekeeping' signals (nutrients, fullness, normal regulation) to the brainstem, while **spinal/[[DRG]]** afferents are weighted toward **mechanical and noxious** signals — strong distension, injury, inflammation — i.e. much of visceral pain.

flag.note: This labor split is a useful rule of thumb, not absolute — both systems carry mechanical and chemical information, with overlap.

steps.prompt: A patient has intense, cramping pain from an inflamed, over-distended colon. Which afferent system most likely carries it?
options: Enteric neurons alone, with no extrinsic afferents
Sympathetic efferent fibers in the splanchnic nerves
steps.explanation: Noxious mechanical and inflammatory visceral signals are weighted toward the spinal/DRG line, which dominates the distal colon. Vagal afferents lean toward physiological regulation.

variants.setup: The distal colon is inflamed and painfully distended.
variants.prompt: Which system most likely carries that pain?
variants.reveal: Visceral pain from the distal gut rides the spinal/DRG line.

steps.setup: After a normal meal, your brain registers nutrients and fullness without any pain.
steps.prompt: Which afferent system is the likeliest main reporter here?
options: Spinal (DRG) afferents to the spinal cord
Enteric neurons, with no signal to the brain
Taste cells in the mouth, during the meal
steps.reveal: Routine nutrient and fullness signaling leans vagal, reporting to the brainstem — the 'housekeeping' side of interoception. Spinal afferents contribute, but are weighted toward strong and noxious signals.

sources.note: A gut-brain neural circuit for rapid nutrient sensing (vagal transduction).
Spinal (DRG) vs vagal innervation of the gut; the DRG side is the frontier.
